column1: # Step 2 (02-rdd-to-dataset): m1..m4, and the four rules that are not
# requirements.
# The step's claim is one sentence: fifteen named classes take their terminal
# result through the SQL engine instead of taking it off an RDD. The evidence is
# two facts about each class, and each requirement below asks for both.
# The first is the runtime one -- `probe job <row>#<id>`, whose value is the SQL
# execution the job ran inside, `-` for no execution, and `forged:<id>` for an
# execution id that no execution ever started (gates/schema.tsv, NOTES 6.2.4).
# It says a job of that class *did* run inside an execution.
# The second is a fact about the artifact: the class no longer references
# `count` or `reduce` on anything in `org.apache.spark.api.java`. It says the
# terminal result is no longer taken off an RDD. It is deliberately not an AST
# rule about how the Dataset was built -- `createDataset` and `createDataFrame`
# and `toDF` and `as(Encoders...)` are all the same migration and a gate that
# named one of them would be marking a style. It is a rule about what went
# away, read from the constant pool, where the receiver's type is already
# resolved and a rename cannot hide it.
# Neither fact alone is the claim, which is the round-1 review's finding and the
# reason the pair exists. A job inside an execution, alone, is bought by one
# `SparkSession.range(1).count()` beside an untouched `pdb.count()` -- or by
# writing the listener's own output file, since a candidate's code runs in that
# same driver. An absent `JavaPairRDD.count`, alone, is bought by printing a
# constant. Together they are the step: the count that used to be an RDD action
# is gone, and a job of that class ran inside a SQL execution.
# Why fifteen and not a hundred and forty. Measured (NOTES 6.2.5): 650 jobs run
# on the golden step-1 tree, 342 of them outside any SQL execution, and most of
# those 342 cannot move -- MMTF Hadoop sequence-file reads, CSV schema
# inference and MLlib internals submit execution-less jobs from code that is
# already fully Dataset-shaped. A rule over all 140 rows would be a rule the
# golden solution itself fails. So the denominator is named, and the names are
# the four requirements below: 15 classes, 20 scored rows, 16 of them with a
# Spark job in them.
# The four rows of the twenty with no job to read are named here rather than
# omitted, because an omission is indistinguishable from an oversight:
#   MmtfBenchmark-missing   prints its usage line and then builds a context
#   MmtfBenchmark-noargs    anyway, dying on args[0]: a full probe file, no jobs
#   ReadLocalMmtf-usage     System.exit(1) before the context exists, so the
#   ReadLocalMmtfHadoopFile-usage   probe never runs and there is no file at all
# Two forms of job rule, and which one a row gets is a measurement and not a
# preference. A row whose only terminal action is the count gets the strict
# form -- *no* job of that row outside an execution -- because after the move
# there is exactly one job and it is inside one (the terminal Dataset action
# drags the whole RDD lineage into the execution rather than adding a job
# beside it: NOTES 6.2.5, four shapes, all one job). A row that also prints
# every record with `foreach`, or writes a sequence file, keeps a second job
# that this step does not ask to move -- §6.2.1's argument for leaving the
# reader alone applies to the writer and to a print -- so those rows get the
# weaker form: at least one job inside an execution. Naming which rows are
# which is the whole content of the two `absent` rules.
# id
column5: reason

column1: # --- what is true of the tree before the step, and must still be true after --
# Nine rules, and seven of them read like requirements and are deliberately
# not requirements: no id here begins `m<digit>-`, so score.py reads them as
# standing rules and a FAIL voids the whole reading instead of costing a
# share. That is the right price for each of them.
# The nine prohibitions this step needs are not here: they are in cheats.tsv,
# included beside this file, because their price is different. A red one of
# those zeroes both families rather than voiding this one, and score.py reads
# that list out of the file itself so the two cannot drift apart.
# `reader-returns-rdd` and `reader-not-rewritten` are the other direction: the
# step must not be answered by moving the *reader* into the SQL engine and
# calling the demos migrated. MmtfReader's contract is a JavaPairRDD keyed by
# structure id, 57 of the library's 78 mains are written against it, and a
# Dataset reader over an opaque interface is the Kryo cheat with a different
# owner.
# `replay-probed` is the instrument check, and it is here because every rule in
# this file reads a fact that only exists if the replay ran with the listener
# attached. Without it the reading has two probe files instead of 125, every
# `absent probe.job` rule passes over nothing, and the forgery rule passes
# hardest of all. 100 rather than 125 because a candidate's tree may legitimately
# lose a probe file or two to a class that now exits earlier; a fifth below the
# real number is a check on the verifier, not on the tree.
# `probe-submit-clean` replaces common.tsv's `probe-submit-ok` for this step,
# and the reason is arithmetic rather than strictness. `probe-submit-ok` asks
# for *at least one* `submit.rc 0`, which was the whole reading when the gate
# saw one probe file. At this step it also sees the verifier's own control run
# -- gate.GateMain, which exits 0 by construction -- so a candidate session
# probe that died would leave `probe-submit-ok` green on the control's row.
# This rule asks the other question, over the same fact: no submit reported
# anything but 0. It is stated here rather than as an `override:` because it is
# a different claim, and common.tsv's line is still worth keeping: one says a
# submit happened, this one says none of them failed.
replay-probed
